thread.title: Between Weak iPhones And Ongoing Margin Challenges, Qorvo Can't Catch A Break - Qorvo, Inc (NASDAQ:QRVO)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Between Weak iPhones And Ongoing Margin Challenges, Qorvo Can't Catch A Break - Qorvo, Inc (NASDAQ:QRVO)
text:
I’m sure some Qorvo ( QRVO ) shareholders will take exception with this, but more and more this company is reminding me of that kid we all know from high school who was uncommonly talented but somehow just never managed to put it together. Management certainly bears some responsibility (particularly for the ongoing challenges in hitting margin targets), but other issues outside of their control like weak iPhone unit sales have undermined some of the positive drivers.
Qorvo shares look undervalued by most metrics I track, but I think it is fair to ask if revenue and margin leverage expectations are still too high, particularly as high-end handsets don’t seem to offer the growth they once did. There are still credible drivers in markets like IoT, wireless infrastructure, and even handsets, but I’d like to see at least another quarter before stepping up and buying these beaten-down shares.
A Big Win With A Big Asterisk Qorvo managed a significant win when it got significant mid/high-band PAD share in Apple ’s ( AAPL ) new phones and increased BAW filter content at the expense of Broadcom ( AVGO ). Coupled with increased envelope tracking and a still-leading position in antenna tuning, this latest round of iPhones was supposed to be a strong driver for the company’s RF business.
And then reality smacked the sector again. For the second year in a row, Apple’s new high-end phones haven’t sold as well as hoped. With weaker than expected volume, a host of Apple suppliers including Skyworks ( SWKS ), ams AG ( OTCPK:AMSSY ), Lumentum ( LITE ), Cirrus ( CRUS ), and Qorvo lowered their guidance for the December quarter. With Qorvo, it stings a little more as the company saw the greatest amount of content in the iPhone XR (roughly double that of the XS), only to see the XR underperform the XS.
Making matters worse, after the close on Wednesday Apple warned on its fiscal first quarter, citing weaker iPhone volumes.
Qorvo is now looking at two consecutive upcoming quarters with high-single-digit revenue contraction, and I think there is a risk of double-digit contraction if conditions weaken further. That has likewise sapped some of the near-term margin leverage that management was hoping to deliver (particularly given sizable recent investments into BAW capacity).
The good news, and I do believe there is good news in the RF business, is that Qorvo has been gaining content with multiple vendors. Weakness at Apple hurts a little more because iPhones are typically leaders in terms of high-value content – Apple’s top of the line has RF band counts averaging in the high 30’s, while Samsung and Huawei are in the low-to-mid 30’s, and that means more high-end filter content and so on. Even so, Qorvo has been doing better at Samsung lately and also does uncommonly well among Chinese OEMs, with Huawei now a 10% customer and others including Xiaomi and Vivo using the company’s components.
Whether Qorvo can maintain its newfound strength with Apple is an open question. Broadcom has pledged to win back share in future models and Skyworks has reportedly been sampling BAW filters with some customers (and offering a high level of configurability) and threatening to stretch beyond its historical position in lower-end SAW and TC-SAW filters. The future rollout of fully 5G phones should offer another boost to the addressable market (with a filter content increase of roughly 50%), but the risk of new market entrants (Skyworks, and maybe someday Qualcomm ( QCOM ) /TDK and/or Akoustis ( AKTS ) ) could see some of those benefits competed away with lower prices.
IDP Still Appealing, But It Will Take Time I’m still generally bullish on Qorvo’s Infrastructure and Defense Products segment (or IDP), and I believe this opportunity is often overlooked in the Street’s obsession with the near-term outlook for mobile RF components.
Like Texas Instruments ( TXN ), Silicon Labs ( SLAB ), and Skyworks, Qorvo is looking at meaningful end-market growth in IoT devices over the coming three to five years, and while I believe Silicon Labs has a stronger overall portfolio in IoT wireless and TI is stronger overall (due to its wireless capabilities and its strength in MCUs), I believe there’s enough room to go around in segments like smart home and industrial IoT to support a healthy growth outlook.
Qorvo also remains strongly leveraged to gallium nitride on silicon carbide, and I believe the company will add to its leading positions today in defense and cable TV with attractive growth opportunities like 5G wireless infrastructure. 5G base stations could be a $1.5 billion-plus market opportunity for Qorvo in three years, driven by products/applications like GaN power amplifiers and GaN-based MIMO antennas. I’d also note that defense could remain an attractive market for Qorvo for some time, with opportunities for GaN-based products in radar and electronic warfare applications.
The Outlook Qorvo named a new head of Global Ops around midyear, hiring Texas Instruments’ former head of worldwide manufacturing Paul Fego. It’s unfair to suggest that there’s been no progress in gross margins at Qorvo, as September quarter adjusted gross margin of 47.7% was clearly better than the 2-year comp of 42.8%, but consider that the 3-year comp is 49.7% and the 4-year comp is 47.8% before celebrating too much. At a minimum, Qorvo has struggled to make consistent progress as quickly as management had hoped, and there is still a need for real improvement.
Considering the revenue outlook, the disappointing volumes for the new iPhone XR clearly doesn’t help and investors should at least consider the risk that this is more like what the future will be – longer replacement cycles and less dramatic volume ramps for new models. The 5G transition may well reaccelerate volumes, but I’m more cautious and conservative now than in the past. I’d also note some risk to the ongoing tensions between the U.S. and China; while most of Qorvo’s China revenue comes from products manufactured in China for the Chinese market, I don’t think you can completely rule out the risk of the U.S. government moving to restrict business relationships with Huawei and ZTE.
I’ve cut my near-term revenue expectations by about 2%, 5%, and 7% for the next three years, and my long-term revenue growth rate has dropped by about a point. I’ve also lowered my near-term margin leverage assumptions, though I still do believe that Qorvo can generate around four points of incremental FCF margin leverage between FY 2018 and FY 2023 and a couple more points beyond that in the years to come, supporting a low double-digit annualized long-term FCF growth rate.
Because discounted cash flow relies more on near-term cash flows, the lower near-term outlook takes about 10% out of my DCF-based fair value. The outlook for lower revenue growth and margins hurts the EV/revenue-based fair value approach even more, and my fair value range moves to the low $70s to the low $80’s for the next 12 months. There’s certainly upside to that range over the longer term, but Qorvo will have to deliver on its margin goals and generate some upside to revenue growth to get there.
The Bottom Line Qorvo has had a rough six months, as have Skyworks, Murata ( OTCPK:MRAAY ), and other iPhone suppliers. I do think the shares are undervalued now, but I’m nervous that the December quarter report will see another cut to March quarter guidance and sentiment today is pretty ugly for semiconductor stocks in general as investors start to worry that the current correction will get ugly on weaker macro trends in 2019. Qorvo deserves credit for taking share from rivals like Skyworks and Broadcom in mobile and deserves more credit for the value of its GaN portfolio/capabilities, but it’s going to take better than mid-single-digit revenue growth and sub-50% gross margins to unlock that potential.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AVGO. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
